// shapes.ts.txt — SCANNED, NEVER RUN. The grammar allows callee shapes that a
// runnable .mjs cannot spell (TS non-null) or that only appear in positions
// the executable fixture has no use for. They are here so the CLASSIFIER is
// measured against the grammar, while the ORACLE is measured against what
// runs. The two denominators are different and saying so is the point.
//
// THE `.txt` TAIL IS LOAD-BEARING. tsconfig's include covers `test/**/*.ts`,
// so a fixture named `shapes.ts` is COMPILED as part of the project — and a
// fixture whose whole job is to hold odd or deliberately degenerate shapes
// cannot also satisfy tsc. The first version of this file was bent to please
// the compiler (`(0, curried)` grew a side effect to dodge TS2695), which
// silently changed the construct under study. The name keeps `.ts` so the
// reader and the scanner still know what language it is.
declare const maybe: ((n: number) => number) | null;
declare const bag: Record<string, (n: number) => number>;
declare const key: string;

export function tsShapes(n: number): number {
  return maybe!(n) + bag[key](n) + bag['fixed'](n);
}


class Base { m(): number { return 1; } }
export class Sub extends Base {
  constructor() { super(); }
  m(): number { return super.m(); }
}

// TWO SITES ADDED AS A MEASUREMENT, 2026-09-04. The grammar allows a member on
// a fresh instance and a member on an inline object literal; the corpus did
// not contain either, so whether the rules already cover them was a GUESS. A
// site turns the guess into a row. Neither needs a rule if `new C()` reaches
// the class and an object literal is its own value — and if it does need one,
// that is worth knowing before the cell is filled from an argument.
export function onNew(n: number): number { return new Base().m() + n; }
export function onLit(n: number): number { return ({ a(m: number) { return m; } }).a(n); }

function curried(n: number) { return (m: number) => m + n; }
export function chained(n: number): number { return curried(n)(n); }
export function seq(n: number): number { return (0, curried)(n)(n); }
export function cond(n: number, f: (x: number) => number, g: (x: number) => number) {
  return (n > 0 ? f : g)(n);
}
// TWO MORE MEASUREMENT SITES, 2026-09-04, and for the same reason as the last
// pair: `maybe!()` and `(c ? f : g)()` refused, and the refusal was about the
// CORPUS — `maybe` is an ambient declaration with no value, and nobody calls
// `cond`, so its parameters carry nothing. Give each a callee the value layer
// can actually reach and the question becomes about the model instead.
const notNull = curried;
export function useNonNull(n: number): number { return notNull!(n)(n); }
export function useCond(n: number): number { return cond(n, curried(1), curried(2)); }

// a TS cast in the callee position. `s_parenthesized` gets no site on purpose:
// measured 2026-09-04, babel does not emit ParenthesizedExpression under this
// parser configuration at all — `(f)(1)` is a plain identifier callee — so no
// corpus can produce that shape and it is waived rather than left `absent`.
export function useAs(n: number): number {
  return (curried as (m: number) => (k: number) => number)(n)(n);
}

// FOUR MORE OBJECT POSITIONS, and these are here rather than in alpha.mjs for
// a reason that is about the ORACLE. `(x as T).m()` and `x!.m()` cannot be
// spelt in a runnable .mjs at all. `(await p).m()` and `` `s`.m() `` CAN be,
// and they must not be: neither resolves today — the first waits on the
// control-form item and the second answers through the String prototype, which
// is the standard library — so a runnable site would show up as an edge the
// runtime takes and the model misses, which is UNSOUND. A shape whose residue
// is known and owned belongs in the corpus the oracle does not run.
// EVERY RECEIVER BELOW IS A REAL VALUE, and that is the whole care taken here.
// The first draft wrote `declare const held: Holder | null` and asked whether
// `held!.pick()` resolves — it does not, and the refusal would have been about
// an ambient declaration carrying no value rather than about the model. The
// same trap caught the `(cast as T)` probe an hour earlier and `maybe!()` in
// this very file a day earlier. A site measures the model only when everything
// except the construct under study already works.
const holder = { pick(n: number): number { return n; } };
type Holder = typeof holder;
async function mkHolder(): Promise<Holder> { return holder; }

// A computed callee whose key is a TEMPLATE with no expressions. The value is
// fixed at parse time, and until 2026-09-08 the scanner's four-relation
// contract could not carry it: TemplateElement.value is `{raw, cooked}`, a
// nested OBJECT, and only scalar own properties became ast_attr facts.
//
// THE CONTRACT MOVED and this site had to move with it. It used to read
// `` bag[`fixed`](n) ``, and `bag` is an AMBIENT DECLARATION carrying no value
// — so the call could not resolve however good the key was, and the site
// measured the receiver rather than the key. That is the trap this file's own
// header names, for the fourth time. `holder` is a real object with a real
// method, so what is under study here is the KEY and nothing else.
export function tmplKey(n: number): number { return holder[`pick`](n); }

export function onCast(n: number): number { return (holder as Holder).pick(n); }
export function onNonNull(n: number): number { return holder!.pick(n); }
// `mkHolder()` alone DOES reach `holder` through the return rule, so the only
// thing standing between this site and an edge is the `await` wrapper — which
// is `w_df_control_forms`, and this site is what will show it landing.
export async function onAwait(n: number): Promise<number> {
  return (await mkHolder()).pick(n);
}
// The receiver here is a String, not a value in this program: `concat` answers
// through the built-in prototype. Its residue is the standard library.
export function onTemplate(n: number): string { return `k${n}`.concat('!'); }

// A TAG THAT IS NOT A FUNCTION, and it is here rather than in a runnable file
// for the reason this file exists: `` stampObj`x` `` throws at runtime, so no
// executable fixture can hold it, and without it the `fn_node` guard on the
// tagged-template rule has nothing to bite on — the mutant that drops it
// derives a byte-identical world. `stampObj` is a REAL VALUE and not an ambient
// declaration, which is the care this file's header already demands: the site
// measures the guard only when everything except the guard already works.
const stampObj = { at: 1 };
// ...and NO `: unknown` return annotation, for the same reason the tag in
// alpha.mjs has no rest parameter: it would introduce `tsunknown_keyword`,
// which this vocabulary does not declare. The gate caught both on the first
// full run, which is the gate doing its job and the fixture doing too much.
export function onTagObject(n: number) { return stampObj`k${n}`; }

// AN ITERABLE WHOSE `next` IS NOT CALLABLE, and it is here for exactly the
// reason `stampObj` is. `for (const x of oneShot)` throws at run time — the
// protocol demands a callable `next` — so no executable fixture can hold it,
// and without a site the `fn_node` guard on the for-of's SECOND hop derives a
// byte-identical world when it is deleted. Measured 2026-09-07 before this was
// written: six mutants aimed at the iterator protocol, and that guard was one
// of the two survivors.
//
// THE VALUE IS AN OBJECT LITERAL AND NOT A NUMBER, which is the whole care.
// `{ next: 1 }` would have looked like the same site and measured nothing: a
// numeric literal is not in `node_value_kind`, so `may_be_node` never reaches
// it and the premise BEFORE the guard is what would have failed. The guard is
// only exercised when everything up to it succeeds.
const oneShot = { [Symbol.iterator]() { return { next: { at: 1 } }; } };
export function onIterObject(n: number): number {
  let s = 0;
  for (const x of oneShot) s += n;
  return s;
}

// A COMPUTED KEY THAT IS NOT A WELL-KNOWN SYMBOL, and the second survivor of
// that set. `key_name` in rules/js-structure.rofl reads a computed key through
// a `Symbol` guard, because `obj[Anything.else]` names a property this model
// cannot know — and the corpus contained exactly ONE computed key, the
// protocol's own, so dropping the guard changed no answer anywhere. It is not
// spellable in a runnable fixture for a duller reason than the others: it
// would run perfectly well, and a method the model must NOT name is a method
// the oracle would then see run under a name nobody derived.
const wellKnown = { spot: 'pick' };
export const aliasedKey = { [wellKnown.spot](n: number): number { return n; } };

// A DESTRUCTURED NAME AND A FREE ONE THAT LOOKS LIKE IT. The value arm for
// destructuring ends in `sees_binder`, and that guard had nothing to bite on in
// a runnable corpus: the fixture in alpha.mjs binds `taken` at module scope and
// uses it once, so a binder visible everywhere and a binder visible in its
// region are the same binder.
//
// HERE THEY ARE NOT. `inner` is bound INSIDE `scoped`, and `outside` calls a
// free identifier of the same name — which throws at run time, so no executable
// fixture can hold it. Without the scoping join the model would resolve
// `outside`'s call to the value bound in a function it is not in, and invent an
// edge. This is scope and NOT shadowing: nothing declares `inner` twice, so it
// asks nothing of w_scope_shadowing.
// `fetched` IS A PLAIN FUNCTION AND NOT `curried`, and the first draft used
// `curried`: `inner(n)(n)` is a call ON a call, so the free identifier left
// `s_call_result` — a shape every site of which resolved — carrying a residue
// with no reason, and `shape_unexplained[audit]` said so within one run. A site
// must introduce the construct it tests and NOTHING ELSE, and a second call was
// a second construct.
function fetched(n: number): number { return n; }
const cache = { fetchIt: fetched };

export function scoped(n: number): number {
  const { fetchIt: inner } = cache;
  return inner(n);
}

export function outside(n: number): number {
  return inner(n);
}

export async function dyn(p: string) { return import(p); }

// THE TWO ERASURE MARKERS AN EXPORT CARRIES (w_export_specifier_forms,
// 2026-09-08), and this file is where they can be spelled at all: a `.mjs` has
// no `type` keyword, so the guards in `export_local` (rules/js-dataflow.rofl)
// had NO SITE in the runnable half of the corpus and their mutants would have
// survived for want of one rather than for want of a rule.
//
// NEITHER LINE DECLARES ANYTHING NEW. `Base` and `curried` are already here and
// already reached by the value layer, so with the guard in place these two rows
// derive NOTHING and with it removed they derive a name the module does not
// offer at runtime — which is exactly the difference the mutant measures. A
// fixture that also introduced a function would have moved the census for a
// question that is not about functions.
export type { Base as BaseType };
export { type curried as curriedType };
